Calculus for ML (Derivatives and Gradients)

A derivative measures how fast a function's output changes when one of its inputs is nudged. A gradient collects one such derivative for every parameter of a model, and training uses it to decide how to change each parameter so that the loss goes down.

1Overview

Why it matters

Every model trained by gradient descent, from linear regression to the networks behind large language models, learns by repeating one calculation: work out how the loss would change if each parameter moved a little, then move every parameter the way that lowers it. That calculation is a derivative. The words of this lesson (partial derivative, gradient, chain rule, Jacobian, Hessian) are the words used in every training loop, optimizer setting and framework error message you will meet.

You will rarely differentiate by hand at work, because libraries such as PyTorch do it automatically. What you need is the ability to read what they compute. Without it, common failures stay opaque: a loss that climbs because a sign is wrong or the learning rate is too large for the curvature, a layer that stops learning because its derivative is close to zero, a hand-written loss whose gradient quietly disagrees with its formula. Someone who can reason about the sign and size of a gradient, and check it with a two-line finite difference, finds these faults in minutes.

Before you start

  • Linear Algebra for MLBeginner

What you will be able to do

  • Compute the derivative of a simple function and explain it both as a slope and as a sensitivity.
  • Compute partial derivatives and assemble them into the gradient of a function of several parameters.
  • Apply the chain rule to a composed function and reproduce the gradient of a one-neuron model by hand.
  • Explain why an optimizer moves parameters against the gradient, and how the learning rate and curvature limit the step.
  • State what a Jacobian and a Hessian contain, what shape each has, and where each appears in ML tools.
  • Verify a hand-derived gradient with a central finite difference.

Key terms

Derivative
The slope of a function at one point, which tells you how much the output changes per small unit of change in the input.
Partial derivative
The derivative of a function of several variables with respect to one of them, taken while the other variables are held fixed.
Gradient
The vector of all partial derivatives of a function that returns a single number. It has one entry per input and points in the direction of steepest increase.
Loss function
A formula that turns a model's predictions and the correct answers into one number that measures how wrong the model is. Training tries to make it small.
Chain rule
The rule for differentiating a function built from other functions, which multiplies the derivatives of the individual steps.
Learning rate
The positive number that scales the gradient to give the size of each parameter update. It is usually written with the Greek letter eta.
Jacobian
The matrix of all first partial derivatives of a function with several outputs, with one row per output and one column per input.
Hessian
The square matrix of all second partial derivatives of a function that returns a single number. It describes how sharply the function curves in each direction.
Finite difference
An approximate derivative computed by evaluating a function at two nearby points and dividing the change in output by the change in input.
Automatic differentiation
A technique in which software records the elementary operations of a computation and applies the chain rule to them to produce exact derivatives.

2Explanation

Introduction

You already use the idea behind a derivative whenever you read a speedometer. Distance travelled is a function of time, and speed is how fast that function is changing right now: its slope at this instant. Calculus is the set of tools for working out such slopes exactly.

Take the function f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 and ask how steep it is at x=3x = 3x=3. A slope needs two points, so pick a second point a distance hhh to the right and divide rise by run: f(3+h)−f(3)h\frac{f(3 + h) - f(3)}{h}hf(3+h)−f(3)​. That is the slope of the straight line through the two points, called a secant line.

hhh210.10.010.001
Secant slope876.16.016.001

As hhh shrinks, the slope settles on 6. That limiting value is the derivative of fff at 3, written f′(3)f'(3)f′(3) or dfdx\frac{df}{dx}dxdf​. Geometrically it is the slope of the tangent line, the line that just touches the curve at that point.

The number 6 is best read as a sensitivity: near x=3x = 3x=3, nudging xxx up by a small amount raises fff by about six times that amount. A positive derivative means the output rises when the input rises, a negative one means it falls, and zero means the function is flat at that point.

Machine learning uses exactly this reading. A model's loss is a single number that measures how wrong its predictions are, and it is a function of the model's parameters. Training asks of every parameter: if this one is nudged, does the loss go up or down, and how fast? The answers, collected into one vector, are the gradient, and the training algorithm moves every parameter a small step in the direction that lowers the loss.

This lesson builds that idea in order: derivatives of one variable, partial derivatives and gradients for many variables, the chain rule for functions built out of other functions, and a first look at the Jacobian and Hessian matrices. It uses the vectors and matrices from linear algebra for ML, and it prepares the ground for gradient descent and backpropagation, which are these ideas turned into algorithms.

How it works

The derivative: a slope at one point

The derivative of fff at xxx is the limit of the secant slope as the second point closes in:

f′(x)=lim⁡h→0f(x+h)−f(x)hf'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}f′(x)=h→0lim​hf(x+h)−f(x)​

For f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 the fraction simplifies to 2x+h2x + h2x+h, which tends to 2x2x2x, so f′(3)=6f'(3) = 6f′(3)=6 as the table suggested. In practice nobody takes limits. A few rules cover most functions in ML; the first four are listed in Dive into Deep Learning (opens in a new tab), and the last follows from them.

constant ccc000Terms that do not involve the parameter
xnx^nxnnxn−1n x^{n-1}nxn−1Squared error
exe^xexexe^xexSoftmax
ln⁡x\ln xlnx1/x1/x1/xLog loss
σ(x)=1/(1+e−x)\sigma(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-x})σ(x)=1/(1+e−x)σ(x)(1−σ(x))\sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x))σ(x)(1−σ(x))Sigmoid units, logistic regression

Constants factor out, (c f)′=c f′(c\,f)' = c\,f'(cf)′=cf′, and sums are differentiated term by term, (f+g)′=f′+g′(f + g)' = f' + g'(f+g)′=f′+g′.

Partial derivatives and the gradient

A loss depends on many parameters at once. Here is a small stand-in with two:

L(w1,w2)=w12+w1w2+2w22L(w_1, w_2) = w_1^2 + w_1 w_2 + 2 w_2^2L(w1​,w2​)=w12​+w1​w2​+2w22​

A partial derivative is an ordinary derivative with respect to one variable while the others are treated as constants. It is written with the symbol ∂\partial∂:

∂L∂w1=2w1+w2,∂L∂w2=w1+4w2\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = 2 w_1 + w_2, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2} = w_1 + 4 w_2∂w1​∂L​=2w1​+w2​,∂w2​∂L​=w1​+4w2​

In the first, w2w_2w2​ is a constant, so w1w2w_1 w_2w1​w2​ differentiates to w2w_2w2​ and 2w222 w_2^22w22​ to zero. At the point (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1), where L=8L = 8L=8, the two partial derivatives are 5 and 6. The gradient, written ∇L\nabla L∇L, stacks them into a vector with one entry per parameter:

∇L(2,1)=[56]\nabla L(2, 1) = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}∇L(2,1)=[56​]

The gradient gives a straight-line forecast of the loss after any small move Δw\Delta wΔw: the change is approximately the dot product ∇L⋅Δw\nabla L \cdot \Delta w∇L⋅Δw. Moving by (0.01,−0.02)(0.01, -0.02)(0.01,−0.02) forecasts 5(0.01)+6(−0.02)=−0.075(0.01) + 6(-0.02) = -0.075(0.01)+6(−0.02)=−0.07, and the true change is −0.0693-0.0693−0.0693.

How the gradient tells an optimizer which way to move

For moves of a fixed small length, that dot product is largest when Δw\Delta wΔw points along the gradient and most negative when it points exactly opposite. The gradient is therefore the direction of steepest increase, and its negative is the direction of steepest decrease. Gradient descent steps that way:

w←w−η ∇L(w)w \leftarrow w - \eta \, \nabla L(w)w←w−η∇L(w)

The learning rate η\etaη sets the step length. With η=0.01\eta = 0.01η=0.01 the point (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1) moves to (1.95,0.94)(1.95, 0.94)(1.95,0.94) and the loss falls from 8 to 7.4027, close to the forecast 8−η∥∇L∥2=8−0.01×61=7.398 - \eta \lVert \nabla L \rVert^2 = 8 - 0.01 \times 61 = 7.398−η∥∇L∥2=8−0.01×61=7.39. Google's Machine Learning Crash Course (opens in a new tab) describes the same loop in words: calculate the loss, determine the direction that reduces it, move a small amount that way, repeat. An optimizer reads three things from a gradient:

  • Sign. A positive entry means the loss rises with that parameter, so the parameter is decreased. A negative entry means it is increased.
  • Size. A large entry marks a parameter the loss is sensitive to, and that parameter receives a proportionally larger change.
  • Zero. Where every entry is zero the forecast is flat and the update stops. That happens at a minimum, but also at a maximum, at a saddle point, and wherever a unit has saturated.

The chain rule

Models are functions inside functions: a loss applied to an activation applied to a weighted sum. The chain rule differentiates a composition by multiplying the derivatives of its links. If y=f(u)y = f(u)y=f(u) and u=g(x)u = g(x)u=g(x), then

dydx=dydu⋅dudx\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}dxdy​=dudy​⋅dxdu​

Take y=(3x+1)2y = (3x + 1)^2y=(3x+1)2 and name the inner part u=3x+1u = 3x + 1u=3x+1. Then dydu=2u\frac{dy}{du} = 2ududy​=2u and dudx=3\frac{du}{dx} = 3dxdu​=3, so dydx=6(3x+1)\frac{dy}{dx} = 6(3x + 1)dxdy​=6(3x+1), which is 24 at x=1x = 1x=1. The reading is direct: a nudge to xxx moves uuu three times as far, and near u=4u = 4u=4 each unit of uuu moves yyy by eight.

When a variable reaches the output along several paths, the contributions of the paths add:

∂y∂x=∑j∂y∂uj ∂uj∂x\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = \sum_j \frac{\partial y}{\partial u_j} \, \frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x}∂x∂y​=j∑​∂uj​∂y​∂x∂uj​​

Backpropagation is this rule applied in an economical order. A forward pass computes and keeps every intermediate value. A backward pass then starts at the loss and multiplies local derivatives back towards the parameters, so each shared factor is computed once. The CS231n notes (opens in a new tab) call the process local: each operation needs only its own derivative and the number handed back by the operation after it. The worked example below does one full pass by hand.

Jacobians and Hessians, at intuition level

The same idea extends to functions of other shapes.

A Jacobian describes a function with several outputs, such as a layer. It is a matrix with one row per output and one column per input, and entry (i,j)(i, j)(i,j) is ∂yi/∂xj\partial y_i / \partial x_j∂yi​/∂xj​. For y1=x12x2y_1 = x_1^2 x_2y1​=x12​x2​ and y2=5x1+x2y_2 = 5 x_1 + x_2y2​=5x1​+x2​:

J=[2x1x2x1251]J = \begin{bmatrix} 2 x_1 x_2 & x_1^2 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}J=[2x1​x2​5​x12​1​]

A linear layer y=Wxy = Wxy=Wx has the Jacobian WWW. For vector functions the chain rule becomes a product of Jacobians, as Parr and Howard (opens in a new tab) show. Frameworks do not build those matrices during training. Each operation only multiplies an incoming vector by its own Jacobian, which is why PyTorch's tutorial describes autograd as an engine for vector-Jacobian products.

A Hessian holds the second derivatives of a function that returns one number: entry (i,j)(i, j)(i,j) is ∂2L/∂wi∂wj\partial^2 L / \partial w_i \partial w_j∂2L/∂wi​∂wj​, the rate at which the iii-th gradient entry changes as wjw_jwj​ moves. It measures curvature. For the example loss it is the same at every point:

H=[2114]H = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}H=[21​14​]

Curvature is what the straight-line forecast leaves out. Stepping from (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1) against the gradient with learning rate η\etaη gives exactly

L(η)=8−61 η+127 η2L(\eta) = 8 - 61\,\eta + 127\,\eta^2L(η)=8−61η+127η2

The −61 η-61\,\eta−61η term comes from the gradient and the +127 η2+127\,\eta^2+127η2 term from the Hessian.

The loss is lowest near η=0.24\eta = 0.24η=0.24, and any η\etaη above 0.48 leaves it higher than where it started. Sharper curvature means a smaller safe step, which is why a learning rate that suits one model makes another diverge. A Hessian has n2n^2n2 entries for nnn parameters, so a model with a million parameters would need 101210^{12}1012 of them, a storage cost that Dive into Deep Learning (opens in a new tab) calls prohibitive for deep networks. Deep learning therefore relies mainly on gradients, while tools with few unknowns per decision, such as Newton-type solvers and XGBoost, use second derivatives directly.

Three ways software obtains derivatives

  • Numerical differentiation applies the definition with a small finite hhh, usually in the central form f(x+h)−f(x−h)2h\frac{f(x + h) - f(x - h)}{2h}2hf(x+h)−f(x−h)​. It works on any function you can evaluate, but it is approximate and needs extra evaluations for every parameter. The CS231n notes (opens in a new tab) count 30,731 loss evaluations for a single update of a classifier with 30,730 parameters. Its lasting use is the gradient check: comparing it with a gradient obtained another way.
  • Analytic differentiation means deriving the formula by hand, or with a symbolic tool, and coding it. It is exact and fast but easy to get wrong.
  • Automatic differentiation records the elementary operations a program performs and applies the chain rule to them, which gives exact derivatives up to rounding. Reverse mode, the kind used for training, returns the whole gradient of a scalar loss in one backward pass. The JAX autodiff cookbook (opens in a new tab) puts the cost at about three times one evaluation of the function, with memory that grows with the depth of the computation. Forward mode handles one input direction per pass and suits functions with few inputs.

A gradient check takes a few lines. This one confirms the gradient (5,6)(5, 6)(5,6) of the two-parameter example:

python
def L(w1, w2):
    return w1**2 + w1*w2 + 2*w2**2

h = 1e-5
dL_dw1 = (L(2 + h, 1) - L(2 - h, 1)) / (2 * h)   # vary w1 only
dL_dw2 = (L(2, 1 + h) - L(2, 1 - h)) / (2 * h)   # vary w2 only
print(round(dL_dw1, 6), round(dL_dw2, 6))        # 5.0 6.0

Worked example: The gradient of a one-neuron model, by hand and in code

A single sigmoid neuron with two inputs is the smallest model that needs every idea in this lesson. It computes a weighted sum, squashes it into the range 0 to 1, and is scored by squared error:

z=w1x1+w2x2+b,a=σ(z)=11+e−z,L=(a−y)2z = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b, \qquad a = \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}, \qquad L = (a - y)^2z=w1​x1​+w2​x2​+b,a=σ(z)=1+e−z1​,L=(a−y)2

One training example has inputs x=(1,2)x = (1, 2)x=(1,2) and target y=1y = 1y=1. The parameters start at w=(0.5,−0.3)w = (0.5, -0.3)w=(0.5,−0.3) and b=0.1b = 0.1b=0.1. The task is to find the gradient of LLL with respect to the three parameters and use it to update them.

∂L∂z=∂L∂a⋅dadz=(−1)(0.25)=−0.25\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} \cdot \frac{da}{dz} = (-1)(0.25) = -0.25∂z∂L​=∂a∂L​⋅dzda​=(−1)(0.25)=−0.25 ∂L∂w1=−0.25×1=−0.25,∂L∂w2=−0.25×2=−0.5,∂L∂b=−0.25×1=−0.25\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = -0.25 \times 1 = -0.25, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2} = -0.25 \times 2 = -0.5, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = -0.25 \times 1 = -0.25∂w1​∂L​=−0.25×1=−0.25,∂w2​∂L​=−0.25×2=−0.5,∂b∂L​=−0.25×1=−0.25

The gradient is ∇L=(−0.25,−0.5,−0.25)\nabla L = (-0.25, -0.5, -0.25)∇L=(−0.25,−0.5,−0.25).

Step 4: read the gradient

Every entry is negative, so increasing any of the three parameters lowers the loss. That fits the situation: the prediction 0.5 is below the target 1, and raising zzz raises the prediction. The entry for w2w_2w2​ is twice the others because its input is 2, so the same nudge moves zzz twice as far. As a spot check, raising w2w_2w2​ by 0.01 should change the loss by about −0.5×0.01=−0.005-0.5 \times 0.01 = -0.005−0.5×0.01=−0.005, and recomputing the loss gives a change of −0.00497-0.00497−0.00497.

Step 5: verify in code and take three steps

The script uses only Python's standard library. gradient is the hand derivation above, and numeric_gradient is an independent check by central differences.

python
import math

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-z))

def loss(w1, w2, b, x1=1.0, x2=2.0, y=1.0):
    z = w1 * x1 + w2 * x2 + b      # weighted sum
    a = sigmoid(z)                 # prediction between 0 and 1
    return (a - y) ** 2            # squared error

def gradient(w1, w2, b, x1=1.0, x2=2.0, y=1.0):
    z = w1 * x1 + w2 * x2 + b
    a = sigmoid(z)
    dL_da = 2 * (a - y)            # outer link
    da_dz = a * (1 - a)            # middle link
    dL_dz = dL_da * da_dz          # chain rule so far
    return dL_dz * x1, dL_dz * x2, dL_dz * 1.0   # inner links: dz/dw1, dz/dw2, dz/db

def numeric_gradient(f, params, h=1e-5):
    grads = []
    for i in range(len(params)):
        up = list(params); up[i] += h
        down = list(params); down[i] -= h
        grads.append((f(*up) - f(*down)) / (2 * h))   # central difference
    return grads

params = [0.5, -0.3, 0.1]
print("loss:", round(loss(*params), 6))
print("chain rule:", [round(g, 6) for g in gradient(*params)])
print("numeric:   ", [round(g, 6) for g in numeric_gradient(loss, params)])

lr = 0.5
for step in range(1, 4):
    grads = gradient(*params)
    params = [p - lr * g for p, g in zip(params, grads)]
    print(f"step {step}: params = {[round(p, 4) for p in params]}, loss = {loss(*params):.4f}")

chain rule: [-0.25, -0.5, -0.25]

step 1: params = [0.625, -0.05, 0.225], loss = 0.1029
step 2: params = [0.6949, 0.0898, 0.2949], loss = 0.0561
step 3: params = [0.7377, 0.1755, 0.3377], loss = 0.0375

The two gradients agree, and each update lowers the loss. The first update is w1=0.5−0.5×(−0.25)=0.625w_1 = 0.5 - 0.5 \times (-0.25) = 0.625w1​=0.5−0.5×(−0.25)=0.625, w2=−0.3−0.5×(−0.5)=−0.05w_2 = -0.3 - 0.5 \times (-0.5) = -0.05w2​=−0.3−0.5×(−0.5)=−0.05 and b=0.1−0.5×(−0.25)=0.225b = 0.1 - 0.5 \times (-0.25) = 0.225b=0.1−0.5×(−0.25)=0.225, which moves the prediction from 0.5 to 0.679.

Two details are worth noticing. The straight-line forecast for the first step was 0.25−0.5×0.375=0.06250.25 - 0.5 \times 0.375 = 0.06250.25−0.5×0.375=0.0625, where 0.375 is the squared length of the gradient, yet the loss only fell to 0.1029: a step of this size is long enough for curvature to matter. And the sign carries everything. Adding the gradient instead of subtracting it gives a loss of 0.4613 after one step, nearly double the starting value.

This forward-then-backward routine is what loss.backward() runs in PyTorch for every parameter of a network, whatever its size. 3Blue1Brown's lesson on backpropagation calculus (opens in a new tab) animates the same three-link chain.

Edge cases and limitations

Functions with corners have no derivative at the corner
ReLU, max(0, x), has slope 0 on the left of zero and slope 1 on the right, so its derivative at exactly zero is undefined. The same holds for the absolute value at zero. Frameworks pick a value so that training can continue: PyTorch's autograd notes list the rules it applies in order, including using a subgradient of minimum norm where the function is locally convex. This is harmless in practice because an input lands exactly on the corner very rarely, but it means a gradient check performed right at a corner can disagree with the framework without either being wrong.
A zero gradient does not mean the minimum has been reached
The gradient is also zero at a maximum, at a saddle point and on a flat plateau. A sigmoid unit is the common plateau: its derivative a(1 − a) is at most 0.25 and is about 0.000045 when z = 10, so a neuron that is confidently wrong passes almost no signal back. Before concluding that training has converged, look at the loss value itself and at which factors in the chain are near zero.
The gradient is only a local forecast
A gradient describes the loss in a small neighbourhood. In the lesson's two-parameter example, a step with learning rate 0.01 lowers the loss from 8 to 7.40, almost exactly as forecast, while a step with 0.5 raises it to 9.25 although the direction is the same. If the loss rises or oscillates from the first few steps while the gradient code is known to be correct, the step is too long for the curvature and the learning rate should be reduced.
Finite differences fail for steps that are too large or too small
A large h gives a secant that is not yet the tangent; a tiny h subtracts two nearly equal numbers and loses digits to rounding. For the forward difference of eˣ at x = 1 in double precision, the error is about 1.4e-2 at h = 0.01, falls to about 6.6e-9 near h = 1e-8, and grows back to about 4.6e-4 at h = 1e-13. The central difference reaches about 6e-11 at h = 1e-5. The Ceres Solver documentation describes the same two regimes. For gradient checks use central differences with h near 1e-5.
Long chains multiply many factors, so gradients can vanish or explode
The chain rule gives a product with one factor per layer. Ten sigmoid layers contribute ten factors of at most 0.25 each, and 0.25 to the tenth power is about 0.00000095, so the earliest layers barely move. Ten factors of 2 give 1,024, and the update overshoots. Activation functions with slope 1 on their active side, normalisation layers, residual connections and gradient clipping exist to keep that product near 1.

When to use it, and when something simpler is enough

Use it when

  • You train any model by gradient descent and need to choose or debug a loss function, a learning rate or an optimizer.
  • You write a custom loss, layer or objective and must derive its gradient or confirm that the framework's gradient matches your formula.
  • A library asks you for derivatives directly, as XGBoost does for a custom objective (first and second derivatives) or SciPy does through its jac argument.
  • You want to know how sensitive an output is to each input, for example to explain a prediction with a gradient-based attribution method.

Think twice when

  • The quantity you care about is not differentiable in the parameters, such as accuracy, a tree's choice of split or the number of layers. Its gradient is zero or undefined almost everywhere, so use a smooth surrogate loss or a search method.
  • The function is a noisy or expensive black box with no code to differentiate. Finite differences amplify the noise, and derivative-free methods such as Nelder-Mead or Bayesian optimisation are the better tool.
  • The problem has an exact solution, as ordinary least squares does on a dataset that fits in memory. Iterating with gradients then adds tuning work for no gain.

A simpler alternative. With one or two parameters, evaluate the loss on a grid of values and pick the lowest point; no calculus is needed and a plot shows you the whole surface. This stops being possible quickly, because a grid with 10 values per parameter needs 10 to the power n evaluations, which is already a million for six parameters. A gradient from reverse-mode automatic differentiation costs a few evaluations of the loss however many parameters there are.

Key takeaways

  • A derivative is the slope of a function at a point, and it is best read as a sensitivity that says how much the output changes per small unit of change in an input.
  • A partial derivative varies one parameter while the others are held fixed, and the gradient is the vector of all the partial derivatives of the loss.
  • The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase, so an optimizer subtracts a small multiple of it from the parameters, and that multiple is the learning rate.
  • The chain rule multiplies the derivatives of the links in a composed function, and backpropagation is that rule applied from the loss back to every parameter.
  • A Jacobian holds the first derivatives of a function with several outputs, and a Hessian holds second derivatives, which describe curvature and limit how large a safe step is.
  • Libraries compute gradients automatically, and a central finite difference is the standard independent check on any gradient you derive or code yourself.

Sources for this explanation: [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [18], [9]

3Real-world applications

5 documented uses of Calculus for ML. Each one names the real system, the problem it solves and its tradeoff, with links to the sources.

  1. PyTorch autograd: the chain rule run backwards over a recorded graph
  2. XGBoost: first and second derivatives of the loss set every leaf value and split
  3. Ceres Solver at Google: Jacobians drive pose estimation and bundle adjustment
  4. Integrated Gradients: differentiating a prediction with respect to its input
  5. SciPy minimize: finite-difference gradients when no derivative is supplied

Example 1 of 5

PyTorch autograd: the chain rule run backwards over a recorded graph

PyTorchDocumented in official docs

PyTorch is an open-source deep learning framework. Its tutorial "A Gentle Introduction to torch.autograd" and its "Autograd mechanics" notes describe how the framework computes the gradients used for training, and the reference page for the SGD optimizer documents the update that consumes them. [9][10][11]

The problem

Training a neural network needs the derivative of the error with respect to every weight and bias. The tutorial's example is a pretrained ResNet-18, a long stack of nested functions that nobody would differentiate by hand, and any edit to a model's code would force the derivation to be redone. The framework has to produce those derivatives itself, for whatever Python code the user writes.

Where this topic fits

Autograd sits between the forward pass and the optimizer step of every training iteration. The forward pass produces the loss, loss.backward() fills the .grad attribute of each parameter with the matching partial derivative, and optimizer.step() reads those values to change the parameters.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. During the forward pass, autograd runs each requested operation and also records that operation's gradient function in a directed acyclic graph. The input tensors are the leaves and the loss is the root.
  2. Calling backward on the loss starts at the root, where the derivative of the loss with respect to itself is 1.
  3. Each recorded gradient function multiplies the value arriving from the operation after it by its own local derivative. That is one link of the chain rule, carried out as a vector-Jacobian product, so no full Jacobian matrix is built.
  4. Where one tensor feeds several later operations, the contributions arriving along the different paths are added together, which matches the multi-path form of the chain rule.
  5. When the traversal reaches the leaf tensors, each parameter's .grad holds the partial derivative of the loss with respect to it. Together these values are the gradient.
  6. The optimizer moves each parameter against its gradient, scaled by the learning rate, and the graph is built afresh on the next forward pass.

Why this approach fits

A training loss is one number that depends on a very large number of parameters. Reverse-mode differentiation matches that shape: one backward pass yields every partial derivative at a cost comparable to a few forward passes, where finite differences would need at least one extra forward pass per parameter. Recording the graph while the code runs also means the derivative always matches the program as it actually executed, including loops and branches, so there is no separate derivation to keep in step with the model.

Limitation or tradeoff

The backward pass needs the intermediate values of the forward pass, so memory use grows with the depth of the computation and training needs far more memory than inference. Autograd differentiates the code as written: a mistake in the loss formula yields a correct gradient of the wrong function. At points where an operation has no derivative, such as ReLU at zero, PyTorch substitutes a value chosen by documented rules, and its notes discourage in-place operations because they can overwrite values the backward pass needs. Gradients are accumulated in .grad, so a training loop has to reset them before each backward pass.

What the sources document

  • The tutorial describes torch.autograd as PyTorch's automatic differentiation engine that powers neural network training, and shows a training step on a pretrained resnet18 in which backward is called on the error tensor and an SGD optimizer then takes a step. [9]
  • Autograd keeps a record of tensors and all executed operations in a directed acyclic graph of Function objects in which the leaves are the input tensors and the roots are the output tensors, and tracing the graph from roots to leaves computes the gradients automatically using the chain rule. [9]
  • When backward is called on the root, autograd computes the gradients from each grad_fn, accumulates them in the respective tensor's .grad attribute and, using the chain rule, propagates all the way to the leaf tensors. The optimizer's step then adjusts each parameter by its gradient stored in .grad. [9]
  • The tutorial states that torch.autograd is an engine for computing vector-Jacobian products, and that when the vector is the gradient of a scalar function the product is, by the chain rule, the gradient of that scalar with respect to the inputs. [9]
  • The mechanics notes say the graph is recreated from scratch at every iteration, which allows arbitrary Python control flow that changes its shape and size, and they list the rules applied in order for non-differentiable functions. The SGD page's algorithm ends each iteration by setting the parameters to their previous values minus the learning rate times the gradient term. [10][11]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 2 of 5

XGBoost: first and second derivatives of the loss set every leaf value and split

XGBoostDocumented in official docs

XGBoost is an open-source gradient boosting library. Its tutorial "Introduction to Boosted Trees" derives the training objective, and its tutorial "Custom Objective and Evaluation Metric" shows the interface through which users supply the derivatives of their own loss. [12][13]

The problem

A boosted model is a sum of decision trees, and a tree is not a list of weights that can be nudged. The tutorial says that learning tree structure is much harder than a traditional optimisation problem where you can simply take the gradient. The library also has to support many losses, including squared error, logistic loss and ranking losses, ideally with a single training procedure.

Where this topic fits

Derivatives are computed at the start of each boosting round, before the next tree is grown. The trees built so far are fixed, so each row has a current prediction. The loss is differentiated with respect to that prediction, once and twice, giving a first derivative gig_igi​ and a second derivative hih_ihi​ for every row. Tree growing then works only with those two numbers per row.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. With the earlier trees fixed, treat the loss for row i as a function of one number, that row's current prediction.
  2. Differentiate it once and twice at the current prediction to get g and h for the row. This replaces the loss by a quadratic with the same slope and curvature at that point, a second-order Taylor expansion.
  3. For a candidate tree, add up g and h over the rows that fall into each leaf to get the leaf totals G and H.
  4. A leaf's contribution to the objective is then a quadratic in the leaf's value. Setting its derivative to zero gives the best value, −G / (H + λ): slope divided by curvature, shrunk by the regularisation constant λ.
  5. Score each candidate split with the gain formula, which uses the same totals for the left child, the right child and the parent, and keep a split only if its gain is positive after subtracting γ.
  6. Add the finished tree to the model, update every row's prediction, recompute g and h, and repeat for the next round.

Why this approach fits

Reducing every loss to the same two numbers per row lets one tree-growing algorithm serve all of them: changing the loss only changes how gig_igi​ and hih_ihi​ are computed. Using the second derivative as well as the first means each leaf value comes out of a formula as a Newton-style step, the slope divided by the curvature, so no step length has to be searched for inside a leaf. The totals are plain sums, so they can be accumulated in a single pass over the rows.

Limitation or tradeoff

The method needs a loss whose second derivative is informative. Absolute error has a second derivative of zero wherever it is defined, so the leaf formula has nothing but λ in its denominator, and a saturated logistic prediction also gives an hih_ihi​ close to zero. The quadratic is also only a local approximation of the loss, which is one reason boosting adds many small trees instead of trusting one large step. For a custom objective the derivatives are written by hand, and the documentation itself warns that getting the order of the subtraction wrong makes training error rise.

What the sources document

  • For general losses the tutorial takes the Taylor expansion of the loss up to the second order and defines g_i and h_i as the first and second partial derivatives of the loss with respect to the previous round's prediction for row i. [12]
  • After the constants are removed, the objective for the new tree depends only on g_i and h_i. The tutorial states that this is how XGBoost supports custom loss functions, and that every loss, including logistic regression and pairwise ranking, is optimised by the same solver that takes g_i and h_i as input. [12]
  • For a fixed tree structure the best leaf weight is given as −G_j / (H_j + λ), where G_j and H_j are the sums of g_i and h_i over the rows in leaf j, and the gain of a split is half of G_L²/(H_L + λ) + G_R²/(H_R + λ) − (G_L + G_R)²/(H_L + H_R + λ), minus γ. [12]
  • The custom objective tutorial says the objective function's role during training is to provide gradient information, both first and second order, based on model predictions and observed labels, and its squared log error example returns two arrays, grad and hess. [13]
  • The same page notes that whether the labels are subtracted from the prediction or the other way around is important, and that training error going up instead of down might be caused by this. [13]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 3 of 5

Ceres Solver at Google: Jacobians drive pose estimation and bundle adjustment

Google (Ceres Solver)Documented in an open-source project

Ceres Solver is an open-source C++ library for non-linear least-squares problems. Its documentation, read here from the project's repository, lists its users, explains how derivatives are supplied to the solver and walks through a bundle adjustment problem. [14][15][16][17]

The problem

Bundle adjustment starts from feature locations measured in many photographs and looks for the 3D point positions and camera parameters that minimise the reprojection error, the gap between where each point was observed and where the current estimate projects it. In the tutorial's dataset every observation depends on a nine-parameter camera and a three-dimensional point. No formula gives the answer, so the solver improves an estimate step by step, and for each step it needs to know how every residual responds to every parameter it depends on.

Where this topic fits

The Jacobian is the input to every solver iteration. All residuals are stacked into a vector F(x)F(x)F(x). The solver evaluates FFF and its Jacobian JJJ at the current estimate, replaces the problem by the linear model F(x+Δx)≈F(x)+J(x) ΔxF(x + \Delta x) \approx F(x) + J(x)\,\Delta xF(x+Δx)≈F(x)+J(x)Δx, solves that linear least-squares problem for the correction Δx\Delta xΔx, and repeats.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Write each observation as a residual function that projects the 3D point through the camera model and subtracts the observed image position. It has 2 outputs and 12 inputs.
  2. Its Jacobian therefore has 2 rows and 12 columns, held as a 2 × 9 block for the camera and a 2 × 3 block for the point. Each entry is the partial derivative of one residual with respect to one parameter.
  3. Obtain those derivatives. Ceres accepts hand-coded formulas, finite differences, or automatic differentiation, in which the same templated residual code is run on a special number type so that derivatives are carried along with values.
  4. Combine the residuals and the Jacobian into the gradient of the objective, JᵀF, and into JᵀJ, which stands in for the Hessian so that no second derivatives have to be computed.
  5. Solve for the step with a trust-region method such as Levenberg-Marquardt, which keeps the step inside a region where the linear model can be trusted.
  6. Compare the reduction in error that was achieved with the reduction the linear model predicted, enlarge or shrink the trust region accordingly, and iterate.

Why this approach fits

A least-squares problem has many outputs, one per residual, so its natural derivative object is a Jacobian and not a single gradient. The squared-error structure then lets the solver obtain curvature information from first derivatives alone, through J⊤JJ^\top JJ⊤J. Each residual touches one camera and one point, so almost all of the Jacobian is zero and large problems stay tractable. Automatic differentiation removes the most error-prone part of the work, the hand derivation of a projection through a rotation, which the tutorial calls a bit of a pain.

Limitation or tradeoff

The linear model is accurate only near the current estimate, which is why the step is confined to a trust region and why a poor starting estimate can lead to a poor answer: the documentation says global minimisation is intractable and the solver settles for a local minimum. The Jacobian also has to be correct and cheap. Finite-difference Jacobians cost extra residual evaluations for every parameter and have limited accuracy, which is why the documentation advises against them except as a last resort.

What the sources document

  • The Users page states that at Google, Ceres is used to estimate the pose of Street View cars, aircrafts and satellites, to build 3D models for PhotoTours, to stitch panoramas on Android and iOS, and to solve bundle adjustment and SLAM problems in ARCore. [14]
  • The page "On Derivatives" says Ceres, like all gradient based optimisation algorithms, depends on evaluating the objective function and its derivatives at arbitrary points, that defining the objective and its Jacobian is the principal task of the user, and that correct and efficient computation of the Jacobian is the key to good performance. [15]
  • The same page lists three ways to supply derivatives (analytic, numeric by finite differences, and automatic using C++ templates and operator overloading) and advises using automatic derivatives and avoiding numeric derivatives except as a measure of last resort. [15]
  • The solver documentation defines the Jacobian of the residual vector F(x) as an m × n matrix whose entry (i, j) is the derivative of f_i with respect to x_j, gives the gradient as J(x)ᵀF(x), and builds each step from the linearisation F(x + Δx) ≈ F(x) + J(x)Δx. [16]
  • In the bundle adjustment tutorial each residual depends on a three-dimensional point and a nine-parameter camera, the cost function is declared as AutoDiffCostFunction<SnavelyReprojectionError, 2, 9, 3>, and the text says computing the analytic Jacobian is a bit of a pain and automatic differentiation makes life much simpler. [17]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 4 of 5

Integrated Gradients: differentiating a prediction with respect to its input

TensorFlow and CaptumDocumented in official docs

Integrated Gradients is an attribution method from the paper "Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks". TensorFlow's tutorial implements it for an Inception V1 image classifier, and Captum, the interpretability library for PyTorch, ships it as the IntegratedGradients class. [19][20][21]

The problem

After a network has classified an image, a practitioner wants to know which pixels the prediction depended on, in order to understand feature importance, spot skewed data or debug the model. The weights are fixed at this point, so the question is about the input. The obvious answer, the gradient of the class probability with respect to the pixels of the image itself, is unreliable: the tutorial explains that gradients describe only local changes and can saturate, shrinking towards zero for the very pixels the model relies on.

Where this topic fits

The method runs after training, when an explanation is requested. The same automatic differentiation that produces parameter gradients during training is asked for a different derivative: the partial derivative of one output, the probability of the target class, with respect to every input feature, with the weights held constant. Integrated Gradients evaluates that input gradient at many points between a baseline input and the real input and combines the results.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Choose a baseline input that stands for the absence of signal. The TensorFlow tutorial uses a black image whose pixel values are all zero.
  2. Build m interpolated inputs on the straight line from the baseline to the real input.
  3. For each interpolated input, run a forward pass and ask the framework for the gradient of the target class probability with respect to the input pixels. The tutorial does this with tf.GradientTape.
  4. Average those gradients. This is a Riemann-sum approximation of the integral of the gradient along the path.
  5. Multiply the average, feature by feature, by the difference between the input and the baseline to get one attribution per feature.
  6. Check the approximation. The attributions should add up to the model's output at the input minus its output at the baseline, and Captum can return the remaining gap as a convergence delta. If the gap is large, use more steps.

Why this approach fits

A derivative with respect to an input is a direct statement about how the output responds to that feature, and automatic differentiation delivers it for every feature in one backward pass, so the method scales to images with many thousands of pixels and needs no change to the model. Integrating along a path repairs the main weakness of a single gradient. In the teaching example the plain gradient at the input is about 0.013 and −0.007 because the sigmoid has saturated, although the first feature is what moved the output from 0.5 to 0.993; the integrated version assigns it 0.59.

Limitation or tradeoff

The tutorial lists two limits: the attributions explain individual examples and are not global feature importances for a dataset, and they do not describe interactions between features. The result also depends on the baseline, which the tutorial says plays a central role in interpreting the attributions. The model must be differentiable, so the method does not apply to tree ensembles. Each explanation costs one forward and one backward pass per interpolation step, and too few steps leave an approximation error: in the teaching example 50 steps leave the attributions 2.5 % short of the exact total.

What the sources document

  • The TensorFlow tutorial says Integrated Gradients aims to explain the relationship between a model's predictions in terms of its features, with use cases including understanding feature importances, identifying data skew and debugging model performance. [19]
  • The tutorial uses an Inception V1 model pre-trained on ImageNet and computes, with tf.GradientTape, the gradient of the predicted probability of the target class with respect to images interpolated between a black baseline image and the original image. [19]
  • It explains that gradients only describe local changes in the model's prediction function with respect to pixel values, and that the gradient for a pixel can saturate, becoming increasingly small and even going to zero. [19]
  • The paper's abstract says the method requires no modification to the original network, needs only a few calls to the standard gradient operator, and was applied to a couple of image models, a couple of text models and a chemistry model. [20]
  • Captum documents IntegratedGradients as approximating the integral of gradients of the model's output with respect to the inputs along the straight-line path from given baselines to the inputs, with a default of 50 steps and an option to return the convergence delta. [21]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 5 of 5

SciPy minimize: finite-difference gradients when no derivative is supplied

SciPyDocumented in official docs

SciPy is the standard open-source scientific computing library for Python. The reference page for scipy.optimize.minimize, the optimisation tutorial and the reference page for check_grad describe how its optimisers obtain derivatives and how a user can verify them. [22][23][24]

The problem

A general-purpose optimiser is handed arbitrary Python functions: a simulation, a likelihood, the error of a curve fit. Methods that use the gradient, such as BFGS, need far fewer function evaluations than derivative-free ones, but many users have no derivative code for their function, and those who write it by hand often get it wrong.

Where this topic fits

The derivative is needed inside every iteration of a gradient-based method. If the caller passed a gradient function through the jac argument, SciPy calls it. If not, SciPy falls back on the definition of the derivative with a small finite step, evaluating the objective again for each parameter. The helper check_grad applies the same approximation as a test of a user-written gradient.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. The caller passes an objective function of a parameter vector and, optionally, jac, a function that returns the gradient vector.
  2. When jac is missing, SciPy perturbs one parameter at a time by a small step h and forms the change in the objective divided by h. This forward difference is done for each of the n parameters.
  3. The method, BFGS by default for a problem without bounds or constraints, uses the gradient to choose a search direction and uses the way the gradient changes from one iteration to the next to build up an estimate of curvature, so the user never supplies second derivatives.
  4. Methods such as Newton-CG go further and use the Hessian, or only products of the Hessian with a vector, supplied by the user or estimated by finite differences.
  5. Before trusting a hand-written jac, the user calls check_grad, which returns the size of the difference between the analytic gradient and the finite-difference one.

Why this approach fits

Finite differences need nothing except the ability to evaluate the function, so they work on black-box code that no automatic differentiation tool can see into. With a handful to a few hundred parameters, one extra evaluation per parameter is affordable, and the tutorial notes that BFGS typically still needs fewer function calls than the Nelder-Mead simplex method even when it has to estimate the gradient.

Limitation or tradeoff

The cost grows in step with the number of parameters, which rules the approach out for neural networks. Accuracy is limited as well: the forward-difference error shrinks only in proportion to hhh, and hhh cannot be made tiny because of rounding, so about eight correct digits is the best that double precision allows, as the plot shows. If the objective is noisy, for example a simulation with a random component or an inner solver with a loose tolerance, dividing by a small hhh amplifies the noise and the optimiser can stall or wander.

What the sources document

  • The minimize reference says jac may be a callable that returns the gradient vector, that if it is None or False the gradient will be estimated using 2-point finite difference estimation with an absolute step size, and that the keywords '2-point', '3-point' and 'cs' select a finite difference scheme with a relative step size. [22]
  • The tutorial says BFGS uses the gradient of the objective function in order to converge more quickly, that a gradient not given by the user is estimated using first-differences, and that BFGS typically requires fewer function calls than the simplex algorithm even when the gradient must be estimated. [23]
  • In the tutorial's five-variable Rosenbrock example, Nelder-Mead reports 339 iterations and 571 function evaluations, while BFGS given the analytic gradient reports 25 iterations (marked as may vary), 30 function evaluations and 30 gradient evaluations. [23]
  • The tutorial describes Newton-CG as based on fitting the function locally to a quadratic form built from the gradient and the Hessian, a matrix of second derivatives, and notes that only the product of the Hessian with an arbitrary vector needs to be available to the routine. [23]
  • check_grad is documented as checking the correctness of a gradient function by comparing it against a forward finite-difference approximation and returning the 2-norm of the difference, with a default step of sqrt(np.finfo(float).eps), approximately 1.49e-08. [24]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

4Common mistakes

  1. Stepping along the gradient instead of against it, often because the error was written as target minus prediction.

    Why it causes problems
    The gradient points uphill. Adding it, or flipping the sign of the error term in a hand-written derivative, raises the loss at every step, and with any sizeable learning rate the parameters run away.
    How to recognise it
    The loss rises from the very first update, even with a tiny learning rate. In the worked example, adding the gradient takes the loss from 0.25 to 0.46 in one step. XGBoost's guide to custom objectives names the order of the subtraction as a possible reason for training error going up.
    How to fix it
    Write the update as the parameter minus the learning rate times the gradient, define the error as prediction minus target before differentiating, and run a gradient check on every hand-written derivative.

  2. Dropping a link of the chain rule, such as the derivative of the activation or the factor contributed by the input.

    Why it causes problems
    The gradient often keeps the right sign, so training appears to work, but its entries have the wrong sizes. Parameters are updated in the wrong proportions, convergence is slow or stalls, and the fault is easy to mistake for a badly chosen learning rate.
    How to recognise it
    A gradient check shows a mismatch by a constant factor, or by a factor that changes with the input. In the worked example, leaving out da/dz would give (−1, −2, −1) in place of (−0.25, −0.5, −0.25).
    How to fix it
    Name every intermediate quantity, write one local derivative per operation as in the worked example's table, and multiply them in order. Compare the result with central differences before using it.

  3. Trusting a hand-coded gradient because the loss goes down for the first few steps.

    Why it causes problems
    A gradient that is right in most components still lowers the loss for a while. The wrong component then drags the parameters away, and training degrades or diverges later, far from the cause.
    How to recognise it
    Compute the relative error between the analytic and the numerical gradient for each component separately. In the first exercise the bias component has the wrong sign, the loss still falls for two steps, and it ends near 8.6 where the corrected gradient reaches 0.52.
    How to fix it
    Make a central-difference gradient check part of the tests for any custom loss or layer, at several random parameter values, and expect a relative error of about one in a million or smaller.

  4. Treating a gradient near zero as proof that training has converged.

    Why it causes problems
    The gradient is also near zero on plateaus and where units have saturated. Stopping there leaves a model that is confidently wrong, and lowering the learning rate, the usual reaction to a stall, makes the stall worse.
    How to recognise it
    The loss is still high while the gradient is tiny. Inspect the factors of the chain: a sigmoid output close to 0 or 1 makes a(1 − a) close to zero, and a ReLU unit whose input is negative for every example passes back exactly zero.
    How to fix it
    Judge convergence by the loss and a validation metric, not by the gradient alone. For saturated outputs, pair a sigmoid with log loss, whose derivative with respect to z is simply a − y, and for hidden units use better initialisation or an activation that does not saturate.

  5. Choosing a learning rate with no regard to curvature, then reading the divergence as a bug in the gradient.

    Why it causes problems
    The gradient is a local forecast. A step longer than the curvature allows overshoots the valley, the loss rises, and each further step overshoots by more, ending in very large values or NaN.
    How to recognise it
    The loss oscillates or grows although a gradient check passes, and it behaves normally when the learning rate is divided by ten. In the second exercise a rate of 0.19 converges, while a rate of 0.21 ends with a loss above 226 after 20 steps.
    How to fix it
    Lower the learning rate until the loss falls steadily, standardise the input features so that curvature is similar in every direction, and consider an optimizer that adapts the step for each parameter.

Requirements

  • Derive both partial derivatives on paper before writing any code, showing each link of the chain.

  • Report a relative error per component, computed as the absolute difference divided by the larger of the two absolute values.
  • Identify which component is wrong and say what kind of mistake it is.
  • Compare the loss after 200 steps for the colleague's gradient and for the corrected gradient.

The derivation gives ∂L/∂w=14∑(pi−yi)xi\partial L / \partial w = \frac{1}{4} \sum (p_i - y_i) x_i∂L/∂w=41​∑(pi​−yi​)xi​ and ∂L/∂b=14∑(pi−yi)\partial L / \partial b = \frac{1}{4} \sum (p_i - y_i)∂L/∂b=41​∑(pi​−yi​). At (0.2,−0.4)(0.2, -0.4)(0.2,−0.4) the loss is 0.647509 and the numerical gradient is about (−0.231297,−0.012397)(-0.231297, -0.012397)(−0.231297,−0.012397). The colleague's value for ∂L/∂w\partial L / \partial w∂L/∂w matches it to a relative error of about 10−1110^{-11}10−11, but their value for ∂L/∂b\partial L / \partial b∂L/∂b is +0.012397+0.012397+0.012397: the right size with the wrong sign, a relative error of 2. With the corrected gradient the loss falls to about 0.5206 after 200 steps, at roughly w=1.488w = 1.488w=1.488 and b=−2.579b = -2.579b=−2.579. With the colleague's gradient the loss falls for two steps and then climbs, ending near 8.6.

Hint 1

For one example write the loss as −[y ln p + (1 − y) ln(1 − p)]. Its derivative with respect to p is −y/p + (1 − y)/(1 − p), and the derivative of p with respect to z is p(1 − p). Multiply the two and simplify.

Hint 2

A relative error near one in ten million or smaller means the two gradients agree. An error near 1 suggests a missing term or factor, and an error of exactly 2 means the two numbers are equal in size with opposite signs.

Hint 3

Do not judge a gradient only by whether the loss falls at first. A gradient that is right in one component can lower the loss for a few steps.

Show solution

Derivation. For one example, let z=wx+bz = wx + bz=wx+b, p=σ(z)p = \sigma(z)p=σ(z) and ℓ=−[yln⁡p+(1−y)ln⁡(1−p)]\ell = -[y \ln p + (1 - y) \ln(1 - p)]ℓ=−[ylnp+(1−y)ln(1−p)]. The chain has three links:

dℓdp=−yp+1−y1−p=p−yp(1−p),dpdz=p(1−p),∂z∂w=x,∂z∂b=1\frac{d\ell}{dp} = -\frac{y}{p} + \frac{1 - y}{1 - p} = \frac{p - y}{p(1 - p)}, \qquad \frac{dp}{dz} = p(1 - p), \qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial w} = x, \quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial b} = 1dpdℓ​=−py​+1−p1−y​=p(1−p)p−y​,dzdp​=p(1−p),∂w∂z​=x,∂b∂z​=1

Multiplying the first two cancels p(1−p)p(1 - p)p(1−p) and leaves dℓdz=p−y\frac{d\ell}{dz} = p - ydzdℓ​=p−y. Therefore ∂ℓ∂w=(p−y) x\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial w} = (p - y)\,x∂w∂ℓ​=(p−y)x and ∂ℓ∂b=p−y\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial b} = p - y∂b∂ℓ​=p−y. The loss LLL is the average over the four examples, and the derivative of an average is the average of the derivatives:

∂L∂w=14∑i(pi−yi) xi,∂L∂b=14∑i(pi−yi)\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = \frac{1}{4} \sum_i (p_i - y_i)\,x_i, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = \frac{1}{4} \sum_i (p_i - y_i)∂w∂L​=41​i∑​(pi​−yi​)xi​,∂b∂L​=41​i∑​(pi​−yi​)

Code.

python
import math

xs = [0.5, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0]
ys = [0, 1, 0, 1]

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z))

def loss(w, b):
    total = 0.0
    for x, y in zip(xs, ys):
        p = sigmoid(w * x + b)
        total += -(y * math.log(p) + (1 - y) * math.log(1 - p))
    return total / len(xs)

def colleague_gradient(w, b):
    ps = [sigmoid(w * x + b) for x in xs]
    grad_w = sum((p - y) * x for p, x, y in zip(ps, xs, ys)) / len(xs)
    grad_b = sum(y - p for p, y in zip(ps, ys)) / len(xs)      # the bug is here
    return grad_w, grad_b

def correct_gradient(w, b):
    ps = [sigmoid(w * x + b) for x in xs]
    grad_w = sum((p - y) * x for p, x, y in zip(ps, xs, ys)) / len(xs)
    grad_b = sum(p - y for p, y in zip(ps, ys)) / len(xs)
    return grad_w, grad_b

def numeric_gradient(f, w, b, h=1e-5):
    grad_w = (f(w + h, b) - f(w - h, b)) / (2 * h)
    grad_b = (f(w, b + h) - f(w, b - h)) / (2 * h)
    return grad_w, grad_b

def relative_error(a, n):
    return abs(a - n) / max(abs(a), abs(n), 1e-12)

w, b = 0.2, -0.4
print(f"loss at start: {loss(w, b):.6f}")
numeric = numeric_gradient(loss, w, b)
for name, grad_fn in [("colleague", colleague_gradient), ("corrected", correct_gradient)]:
    analytic = grad_fn(w, b)
    for label, a, n in zip(["dL/dw", "dL/db"], analytic, numeric):
        print(f"{name:9s} {label}: analytic {a:+.6f}  numeric {n:+.6f}  relative error {relative_error(a, n):.1e}")

def train(grad_fn, steps=200, lr=0.5):
    w, b = 0.2, -0.4
    for _ in range(steps):
        gw, gb = grad_fn(w, b)
        w, b = w - lr * gw, b - lr * gb
    return w, b, loss(w, b)

for name, grad_fn in [("corrected", correct_gradient), ("colleague", colleague_gradient)]:
    w_end, b_end, loss_end = train(grad_fn)
    print(f"{name:9s} after 200 steps: w = {w_end:.4f}, b = {b_end:.4f}, loss = {loss_end:.6f}")
text
loss at start: 0.647509
colleague dL/dw: analytic -0.231297  numeric -0.231297  relative error 2.4e-12
colleague dL/db: analytic +0.012397  numeric -0.012397  relative error 2.0e+00
corrected dL/dw: analytic -0.231297  numeric -0.231297  relative error 2.4e-12
corrected dL/db: analytic -0.012397  numeric -0.012397  relative error 1.4e-10
corrected after 200 steps: w = 1.4881, b = -2.5789, loss = 0.520571
colleague after 200 steps: w = -9.9523, b = 29.0690, loss = 8.605015

The last digits of the small relative errors can differ between machines.

Reading the result. The colleague wrote y - p where the derivation gives p - y, so the bias component has the correct size and the opposite sign. Every step therefore moves bbb uphill. The loss still falls on the first two steps (0.6475, 0.6269, 0.6221) because the www component is correct and about nineteen times larger at the start, and then it rises steadily as bbb runs away. Watching the loss for a couple of steps would have missed the bug; the gradient check finds it immediately.

Check your answer

  • Does your derivation reach p − y for the derivative with respect to z of one example's loss, before averaging?
  • Is your numerical gradient at (0.2, −0.4) approximately (−0.231297, −0.012397)?
  • Does the relative error come out as 2 for the colleague's bias component and far below one in a million for the weight component?
  • Does the corrected run end with a loss near 0.5206 and the colleague's run with a loss near 8.6?
  • Can you explain why the colleague's version still lowered the loss on its first two steps?

Exercise 2

Predict the largest safe learning rate from the Hessian

AnalysisIntermediateAbout 40 min (estimate)Hypothetical scenario

A loss with two parameters is shaped like a long, narrow valley:

L(w1,w2)=12w12+5w22L(w_1, w_2) = \tfrac{1}{2} w_1^2 + 5 w_2^2L(w1​,w2​)=21​w12​+5w22​

Gradient descent starts at (w1,w2)=(4,1)(w_1, w_2) = (4, 1)(w1​,w2​)=(4,1), where the loss is 13.

  1. Compute the gradient and the Hessian. What are they at the starting point?
  2. Take two gradient-descent steps by hand with learning rate η=0.1\eta = 0.1η=0.1. Give the parameters and the loss after each step.
  3. Show that every step multiplies w1w_1w1​ by (1−η)(1 - \eta)(1−η) and w2w_2w2​ by (1−10η)(1 - 10\eta)(1−10η). For which learning rates does w2w_2w2​ grow instead of shrinking?
  4. Predict what happens after 20 steps for η\etaη = 0.05, 0.1, 0.19 and 0.21, then check with a short script. Standard-library Python is enough.
  5. Explain in two or three sentences why no single learning rate suits both parameters, and name one remedy.

Requirements

  • Give the gradient as a vector and the Hessian as a 2 by 2 matrix.
  • Show the arithmetic for both hand-computed steps.
  • Derive the per-step multipliers from the update rule, not from the output of the script.
  • State the threshold learning rate and relate it to the largest entry on the diagonal of the Hessian.
  • Report both parameters and the loss after 20 steps for all four learning rates.

Expected behaviour

The gradient is (w1,10w2)(w_1, 10 w_2)(w1​,10w2​), which is (4,10)(4, 10)(4,10) at the start, and the Hessian is the diagonal matrix with entries 1 and 10 at every point. With η=0.1\eta = 0.1η=0.1 the first step lands on (3.6,0)(3.6, 0)(3.6,0) with loss 6.48 and the second on (3.24,0)(3.24, 0)(3.24,0) with loss 5.2488. w2w_2w2​ grows when η\etaη is above 0.2, which is 2 divided by the largest curvature, 10. After 20 steps the losses are about 1.0281 for η=0.05\eta = 0.05η=0.05, 0.1182 for 0.1, 0.0757 for 0.19 and 226.30 for 0.21.

Hint 1

Substitute the gradient into the update rule one coordinate at a time. Each coordinate's update involves only that coordinate.

Hint 2

A quantity that is multiplied by m at every step shrinks when the absolute value of m is below 1, and it changes sign at every step when m is negative.

Hint 3

For the remedy, ask what change of variable would make the two diagonal entries of the Hessian equal.

Show solution

1. Gradient and Hessian. Differentiating term by term gives ∂L∂w1=w1\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = w_1∂w1​∂L​=w1​ and ∂L∂w2=10w2\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2} = 10 w_2∂w2​∂L​=10w2​, so ∇L(4,1)=(4,10)\nabla L(4, 1) = (4, 10)∇L(4,1)=(4,10). Differentiating again gives second derivatives of 1 and 10, and the mixed derivative is zero because neither first derivative contains the other variable:

H=[10010]H = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 \end{bmatrix}H=[10​010​]

The Hessian does not depend on the point. The loss curves ten times more sharply along w2w_2w2​ than along w1w_1w1​.

2. Two steps with η=0.1\eta = 0.1η=0.1.

Stepw1w_1w1​w2w_2w2​Loss
start418+5=138 + 5 = 138+5=13
14−0.1×4=3.64 - 0.1 \times 4 = 3.64−0.1×4=3.61−0.1×10=01 - 0.1 \times 10 = 01−0.1×10=012(3.6)2=6.48\tfrac{1}{2}(3.6)^2 = 6.4821​(3.6)2=6.48
23.6−0.1×3.6=3.243.6 - 0.1 \times 3.6 = 3.243.6−0.1×3.6=3.24012(3.24)2=5.2488\tfrac{1}{2}(3.24)^2 = 5.248821​(3.24)2=5.2488

3. Multipliers. The update for the first coordinate is w1←w1−ηw1=(1−η)w1w_1 \leftarrow w_1 - \eta w_1 = (1 - \eta) w_1w1​←w1​−ηw1​=(1−η)w1​ and for the second w2←w2−10ηw2=(1−10η)w2w_2 \leftarrow w_2 - 10 \eta w_2 = (1 - 10\eta) w_2w2​←w2​−10ηw2​=(1−10η)w2​. w2w_2w2​ shrinks only when ∣1−10η∣<1|1 - 10\eta| < 1∣1−10η∣<1, that is for 0<η<0.20 < \eta < 0.20<η<0.2. At η=0.1\eta = 0.1η=0.1 the multiplier is zero and w2w_2w2​ reaches its best value in one step. Above 0.2 the multiplier is below −1-1−1, so w2w_2w2​ changes sign and grows at every step. The threshold 0.2 equals 2 divided by 10, the largest curvature.

4. Twenty steps.

python
def loss(w1, w2):
    return 0.5 * w1 ** 2 + 5 * w2 ** 2

def gradient(w1, w2):
    return w1, 10 * w2

for lr in [0.05, 0.1, 0.19, 0.21]:
    w1, w2 = 4.0, 1.0
    for _ in range(20):
        g1, g2 = gradient(w1, w2)
        w1, w2 = w1 - lr * g1, w2 - lr * g2
    print(f"lr = {lr:<4}: w1 = {w1:8.4f}, w2 = {w2:8.4f}, loss = {loss(w1, w2):9.4f}")
text
lr = 0.05: w1 =   1.4339, w2 =   0.0000, loss =    1.0281
lr = 0.1 : w1 =   0.4863, w2 =   0.0000, loss =    0.1182
lr = 0.19: w1 =   0.0591, w2 =   0.1216, loss =    0.0757
lr = 0.21: w1 =   0.0359, w2 =   6.7275, loss =  226.2969

Each row follows from the multipliers. At 0.05, w2w_2w2​ halves at every step and vanishes, while w1w_1w1​ is only multiplied by 0.95, so 4×0.9520=1.4344 \times 0.95^{20} = 1.4344×0.9520=1.434 remains. At 0.19, w1w_1w1​ is nearly gone, but w2w_2w2​ is multiplied by −0.9-0.9−0.9 and still has 0.920=0.12160.9^{20} = 0.12160.920=0.1216 left, so it has become the slow coordinate. At 0.21, w2w_2w2​ is multiplied by −1.1-1.1−1.1 and has grown to 1.120=6.72751.1^{20} = 6.72751.120=6.7275.

5. Why one learning rate is a compromise. The sharp direction caps the learning rate at 0.2, while the flat direction would be solved in one step by a rate of 1, so any allowed rate leaves w1w_1w1​ shrinking by at most 20 % per step. The ratio of the two curvatures sets how bad the compromise is. One remedy is to rescale so that the curvatures match: with v=10 w2v = \sqrt{10}\,w_2v=10​w2​ the loss becomes 12w12+12v2\tfrac{1}{2} w_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} v^221​w12​+21​v2, and a rate of 1 reaches the minimum in one step. Standardising input features has this effect in practice. The other remedy is to divide each coordinate's step by its curvature. Newton's method does exactly that with w−H−1∇Lw - H^{-1} \nabla Lw−H−1∇L, which here gives (4−4/1, 1−10/10)=(0,0)(4 - 4/1,\ 1 - 10/10) = (0, 0)(4−4/1, 1−10/10)=(0,0) in a single step, and adaptive optimizers approximate the idea with a separate step size per parameter.

  • Is your divergence threshold a learning rate of 0.2?
  • Do your four losses after 20 steps match 1.0281, 0.1182, 0.0757 and 226.30 to the digits shown?
  • Can you say which parameter is the slow one at a learning rate of 0.05 and which at 0.19?

    Backpropagation as a local process on a circuit of gates, with fully worked numeric examples, the patterns of add, multiply and max gates in the backward flow, why gradients add where a variable branches, and how to work out gradients of matrix operations by matching dimensions.

    Before the backpropagation lesson, or whenever you need to derive the gradient of a new operation by hand.

    Matrix calculus built up from scalar rules: gradients, Jacobians and their layout conventions, the vector chain rule as a product of Jacobians, and a full derivation of the gradient of a neuron's activation and of a mean-squared-error loss.
    When to use it
    When you start reading papers or framework source code and meet derivatives written with vectors and matrices instead of single variables.
